title: DePIN on Solana: Power Ledger's Peer-to-Peer Energy Network with Co-Founder Dr. Jemma Green
description:
Dr. Jemma Green left a career in London investment banking with an idea about building an eco-village. A former colleague introduced her to John Bullich, who was excited about a new technology she barely understood. Three months later, with her seven-week-old baby in the room and her mum holding the bottle, they started Power Ledger.

Power Ledger makes software for peer-to-peer energy trading. If you have solar panels and your neighbor doesn't, you can sell that electricity directly through your energy supplier instead of letting the grid throw it away. Households can earn income from EV charging, rooftop solar, and the energy they don't use.

After a year of evaluating other technologies, Power Ledger moved to Solana. Ethereum could only process 10 to 15 transactions per second. Solana handles tens of thousands at near-zero cost, and the energy footprint matched what they were trying to build.

"I wanted to make a meaningful contribution to the energy transition. From centralized to a hybrid decentralized system that is truly two-sided, that allows citizens to contribute to energy markets in a meaningful way. That really lights me up."

Learn more at powerledger.io

asr.full_text: I left London where I'd been working in investment banking and I got this idea about building it ecovillage. A former banking colleague of mine introduced me to John Bullich who is my co-founder at Powerledger. He was enthusiastically telling me about blockchain of which I knew very little at that point. I just had a baby seven weeks earlier, I called up my mum and said mum could you come over and hold baby Amelie? And so the four of us, my mum, the baby and John and I sat in my lounge room. I asked what could it do in the case of electricity and we started to work together and 3 months later we set up a company, Powerledger. We make software for tracking and kitto peer trading electricity and energy certificates. That allows citizens and businesses to trade electricity via their energy supplier. Say we live on the same street, and I have solar and you don't. The grid says I don't want that electricity, so they might start to curtail it throwing the energy away, which is a real market failure. In this future state, I could export that and you might use that very cheap electricity and in doing so, avoid it congesting the substation. There is enough generation locally that can be produced that you don't need to get it from elsewhere. You're starting to see people experimenting with EV charging stations in their own home that people can use tokens to be able to use those in charge. So, households can derive income. There's a big role for blockchain and Deepen in that. Our road to Solana was quite interesting. We spent about a year in other technologies and Solana just really stood out. Ethereum could only process 10 to 15 transactions per second whereas Solana can process 30,000 to 50,000 even more. It's super low cost, super energy efficient. I think that was really important to us as well because we didn't want to have a really energy-heavy blockchain with an energy use case. So it was night and day. in energy in the first place is I wanted to make a meaningful contribution to the energy transition from centralised to a hybrid decentralised system that is truly two-sided that allows citizens to contribute to the energy markets in a meaningful way and for me that really lights me up to be a part of that change We've made more good decisions than we have bad and we're still here Really proud that we're in the game, and Forging Ahead.
